figures.alt: A Michigan lakeshore on a rainy spring day. Blue-green lake water and a sandy beach lie on the left. A grassy hill slopes down to the shore with a few bare brown streaks of soil and a small muddy stream running toward the lake. A grey rain cloud hangs overhead.
figures.caption: Rain runs down a Michigan lakeshore hill: bare soil washes toward the lake while grass holds the slope.

figures.alt: Illustration of two adults in everyday jackets looking at a rain garden of native plants in a strip next to a parking lot, in light rain.
figures.caption: A rain garden soaks up some runoff. It helps, but it does not stop all flooding.

figures.alt: Photo of a sloped plastic tray with a sand channel and grass along one bank while water is poured at the top and carries sand down the channel.
figures.caption: The stream tray: compare how much sediment moves with and without plants or stones.

figures.alt: A rainy hillside shown from the side. A grey rain cloud drops rain at the top. On the right, a bare brown slope has muddy water running down it and a grey rock sits at the bottom. On the left, a green grassy slope has roots under the grass that hold the soil in place.
figures.caption: One rainy hill shows all four spheres at work: air, water, rock and soil, and living things.

figures.alt: A cutaway side view of where Earth’s water is. On the left is a large blue ocean with waves. On the right is land with a grey mountain topped by white snow and glacier ice, a layer of light blue groundwater under the soil, and a small lake and a thin river on the green ground.
figures.caption: Where Earth’s water is: mostly salty ocean. The fresh water is mostly ice or underground, and lakes and rivers hold very little.

figures.alt: Interactive: rain falls on a hill that is bare, grassy or stony and the soil moved is counted, with buttons that name the atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere.
figures.caption: Make it rain on a bare, grassy or stony hill and tap the four spheres.

figures.alt: Interactive: predict how many of 100 squares are lakes and rivers, then see 97 ocean, 2 ice, 1 underground and a tiny dot for lakes and rivers.
figures.caption: Predict, then color 100 squares for Earth’s water.

figures.alt: Bar graph, Sediment moved in the stream tray. No plants 12 spoonfuls, Stones 7 spoonfuls, Grass 4 spoonfuls.
figures.caption: Stream-tray test, sediment moved: no plants 12 spoonfuls, stones 7, grass 4.

figures.alt: A grid of 100 squares. 97 are blue for salty ocean water, 2 are yellow for frozen fresh water, 1 is green for fresh water underground. Lakes and rivers are less than one square, shown as a tiny dot.
figures.caption: If all of Earth’s water were 100 squares: about 97 are salty ocean, 2 are frozen fresh water, about 1 is fresh water underground, and lakes and rivers are less than one square, a tiny dot. Almost no liquid fresh water is easy to reach.

figures.alt: Bar graph, Runoff after a storm. Parking lot 10 buckets, Rain garden 6 buckets.
figures.caption: Runoff after a storm: parking lot 10 buckets, rain garden 6 buckets. A rain garden reduces runoff but does not stop all of it.
